strengths: First budget-feasible mechanism with provable approximation guarantees for submodular welfare maximization, addressing a clear open problem in the literature
Novel and sophisticated mechanism design with clever technical innovations: geometric thresholds, singleton candidate protection, value-to-payment ratio control, and disjoint sequence tracking
Rigorous theoretical analysis with careful case decomposition, particularly the element partitioning strategy (Definition 4.2) and threshold bounding (Lemma 4.5)
Improves deterministic approximation ratio for valuation maximization from 1/64 to 1/(12+4√3) while reducing complexity from O(n²log n) to O(n log n)
Comprehensive experimental validation across large-scale networks (up to 265K nodes) demonstrating significant empirical improvements (1.22×–26.41× welfare gain)
All essential economic properties formally established: obvious strategyproofness, individual rationality, budget feasibility, and non-negative auctioneer surplus
Well-organized presentation with clear motivation, appropriate algorithmic exposition, and effective use of appendix for technical proofs
weaknesses: Approximation ratios remain modest in absolute terms (0.0328 for general, 0.0877 for monotone submodular) without context on optimality—paper lacks lower bounds or hardness results specific to budget-feasible welfare maximization setting
Large gap between monotone (0.0877) and non-monotone (0.0328) approximation ratios (2.67×) suggests analysis for general submodular may be loose; no investigation of whether this gap is fundamental
Weaker approximation notion (v(S)−c(S) ≥ γ_w·v(O)−c(O)) vs multiplicative guarantees used without thorough discussion of practical implications or sufficiency conditions
Additive error terms in main theorems (ε/4 in 4.8, ε/3 in 4.10) complicate guarantees; guidance for practitioners on setting ε not provided
Parameter optimization (α, β values) determined via 'optimizing approximation ratio' without confirming global optimality or sensitivity analysis; robustness to parameter choices unexplored
Experimental evaluation limited primarily to influence maximization; claims about broad procurement auction applicability (data acquisition, crowdsourcing, supply chain) only partially validated
BFM-VM variant, while mathematically solid, feels somewhat tangential to main contribution; relationship between welfare and valuation mechanisms could be better motivated
Baseline adaptation strategy (prefix truncation for budget-unconstrained methods) reasonable but imperfect; no exploration of robust alternatives
No sensitivity analysis on network size effects, cost distribution impacts, or oracle evaluation complexity; missing discussion of practical deployment considerations

strengths: First budget-feasible mechanism for submodular welfare maximization with provable guarantees, addressing a meaningful open problem
Technically sound theoretical analysis with clever use of break conditions and geometric thresholds to ensure budget feasibility
Improved valuation maximization bounds (0.0528 vs 0.0156) with reduced time complexity O(n log n)
Comprehensive treatment including both general and monotone submodular functions with proper economic properties
Descending clock auction format provides stronger strategyproofness properties than prior sealed-bid approaches
weaknesses: Approximation ratios are extremely weak (0.0328 for general submodular welfare) with no lower bounds or justification for their practical utility or gap to possible improvements
Theorems include problematic additive error terms (e.g., -ε/4) that can dominate welfare values; no guidance on choosing ε or understanding when additive terms dominate

Experimental validation is questionable: baselines adapted from algorithms not designed for budget constraints using 'longest prefix' truncation, potentially unfairly handicapping them and exaggerating improvements (4.49×)
Limited algorithmic novelty: geometric thresholds and partition arguments are standard techniques; adaptation to welfare appears incremental rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas
Time complexity O(n log(OPT/ε)) depends on unknown optimal welfare OPT, making it impractical without prior knowledge; unclear how practitioners should choose parameters
Single application tested for welfare maximization; missing sensitivity analysis for parameter choices (α, β) and incomplete exploration of budget tightness effects
Inadequate discussion of when weak 0.0328 approximations are practically meaningful or useful; insufficient comparison to hardness results

strengths: Addresses a significant open problem: First budget-feasible mechanism with provable guarantees for submodular welfare maximization in procurement auctions, closing the gap between Deng et al. (2025) which lacked budget feasibility

Novel technical design: Geometrically increasing threshold serving dual purpose (price-setting and welfare benchmarking), singleton candidate with temporal protection, and value-to-payment ratio parameter β are creative solutions

Rigorous theoretical analysis: Complete proofs, elegant partitioning argument (Definition 4.2) for handling excluded elements, appropriate case analysis, and separate improved results for monotone submodular functions (0.0877 vs 0.0328)
Strong improvement for valuation maximization: 3.4× improvement over Balkanski et al. (2022) deterministic ratio (1/(12+4√3) vs 1/64) with quadratic runtime speedup (O(n log n) vs O(n² log n))

Satisfies all standard economic properties: Obvious strategyproofness (stronger than truthfulness), individual rationality, budget feasibility, and non-negative auctioneer surplus in elegant unified framework
Solid experimental validation: Tests on real-world networks (Slashdot, Email, Epinions) showing 1.22×–26.41× improvement with average 4.49× gain, including both oracle queries and wall-clock time
Clear presentation: Well-motivated problem formulation, good narrative flow, appropriate use of appendix for detailed proofs, and comprehensive related work
weaknesses: Weak approximation ratios with no hardness analysis: 0.0328 for general and 0.0877 for monotone welfare maximization are quite weak. No lower bounds provided to assess optimality or gap to hardness, completely unaddressed despite being a critical question

Questionable experimental baselines: Baseline mechanisms (Deng et al. methods) adapted via prefix truncation—unclear if this is fair comparison for unconstrained algorithms. The 26.41× improvement factor seems suspiciously large and raises fairness concerns. No ablation studies on mechanism choices

Limited experimental scope: Only two applications tested (influence maximization, crowdsourcing). No sensitivity analysis for key parameters (α, β, ℓ, ε). Error parameter ε set uniformly to 0.1 without justification or sensitivity analysis

Parameter choices lack intuition: Why initialize ρ₀ = ε/α rather than ε? Why restrict to ℓ ∈ {1,2}? Parameters (α ≈ 2.63, β = 4) appear optimized purely for final ratio without explaining design principles or trade-offs

Running time complexity gap: Theorem 4.1 gives O(n log OPT/ε) complexity. When OPT >> B (possible since welfare can be negative), this could be large. The additive error ε/4 also appears loose but its practical impact is not discussed

Incomplete mechanism analysis: The crucial break condition (Line 13) and Lemma 4.5 lack intuitive explanation. No analysis of performance with extremely tight vs. loose budgets. No discussion of how seller costs relate to optimal solution composition

Non-standard approximation notion: While justified by hardness results, the weak multiplicative approximation v(S) - c(S) ≥ γ_w·(v(O) - c(O)) needs better intuition for why this is the right target versus alternatives (additive approximations, etc.)

Missing important discussions: No lower bounds even informally discussed. Limited clarification of why budget constraints specifically break Deng et al. (2025) techniques beyond coupling allocation-payment. No comparison with simple heuristics. Source code availability claimed but full link not provided
